title: Security Principles for TypeScript knowledge check

questions.prompt: What should happen at an external trust boundary?
options: Cast it to the desired interface and skip validation.
Trust client-submitted roles and ownership fields.
Return secrets in logs to simplify debugging.
Treat incoming data as unknown, validate its structure and policy, then create a trusted domain value.
questions.answer_key: Treat incoming data as unknown, validate its structure and policy, then create a trusted domain value.
questions.explanation: Compile-time types do not validate external values or enforce authorization by themselves.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct about “Security Principles for TypeScript”?
options: A type assertion automatically validates every value at runtime.
The learner should publish hidden solutions so the exercise can grade itself.
The concept should be demonstrated with type safety versus runtime security and checked against its intended contract.
The safest approach is to skip diagnostics and trust the first output.
questions.answer_key: The concept should be demonstrated with type safety versus runtime security and checked against its intended contract.
questions.explanation: The supplied syllabus explicitly includes “Type safety versus runtime security”; connect it to a concrete example and verify the behavior relevant to this lesson.

questions.prompt: What is a good verification step after practicing “Security Principles for TypeScript”?
options: Treat passing a static token check as proof that the program executed correctly.
Check trust boundaries, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
Assume secure handling of external data is unnecessary because the code has type annotations.
Ignore compiler or test failures if the interface looks correct.
questions.answer_key: Check trust boundaries, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
questions.explanation: The syllabus includes “Trust boundaries”. Verification should match the concept: type-level checks, runtime tests, configuration checks or human review as appropriate.
